passages.title: The Big Temple of Thanjavur
passages.text: More than a thousand years ago, the Chola king Rajaraja I ordered the building of a temple at Thanjavur that would announce the power of his empire to the world. The Brihadeeswarar Temple, completed around 1010 CE, is still admired as one of the finest achievements of Tamil architecture. Its tower, or vimana, rises to about sixty-six metres and is built almost entirely of granite. What makes this remarkable is that there is no granite quarry close to Thanjavur. The huge blocks had to be carried from distant places, probably with the help of elephants, carts and ramps of earth. The temple was not only a place of worship. Inscriptions on its walls record the names of dancers, musicians, lamp-keepers and accountants who served it, and the villages that gave it grain and gold. In this way the stone walls act as a kind of register of Chola society. Historians have learnt a great deal about taxation, land grants and daily life from these records. In 1987 the temple was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today, thousands of visitors walk through its gateways every week. Many of them come for prayer; others come simply to stand in its vast courtyard and wonder how people without modern machines created something so grand and so lasting.

passages.title: Pichavaram Mangroves
passages.text: Near Chidambaram, where the Vellar and Kollidam rivers approach the Bay of Bengal, lies one of the most beautiful wetlands of Tamil Nadu: the Pichavaram mangrove forest. Here, small islands covered with dense green trees are separated by a maze of narrow canals. Visitors glide through them in rowing boats, watching kingfishers dive and crabs scuttle across the mud. Mangroves are special trees that can survive in salty, muddy water where most plants would die. Many of them send up breathing roots that stick out of the mud like pencils, while others stand on arching stilt roots. These tangled roots slow down the flow of water and trap silt, so the forest slowly builds and protects the land behind it. Fish, prawns and crabs lay their eggs among the roots, which makes mangroves nurseries for the sea. The value of these forests became clear to many people after the Indian Ocean tsunami of December 2004. In several places along the coast, villages sheltered behind thick mangroves suffered less damage than those on open beaches. Since then, local communities and the forest department have worked together to plant new mangroves and to protect the old ones. Their efforts show that guarding nature is often the cheapest and wisest way of guarding ourselves.

passages.title: The Doctor Who Asked Doctors to Wash Their Hands
passages.text: In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis was a young doctor working in a large maternity hospital in Vienna. The hospital had two wards for mothers giving birth. In the first, run by doctors and medical students, many mothers died of a fever soon after delivery. In the second, run by midwives, far fewer died. Frightened women even begged not to be admitted to the first ward. Semmelweis studied the two wards carefully. He noticed that doctors and students often came straight from examining dead bodies to attend to mothers, while midwives did not. When a colleague died after cutting his finger during such an examination, showing the same signs as the mothers, Semmelweis concluded that some kind of matter from the bodies was being carried on the doctors' hands. He ordered everyone to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients. The death rate in the first ward fell sharply. Strangely, many senior doctors refused to accept his idea. Some were offended by the suggestion that they themselves were spreading disease. Semmelweis died in 1865, largely unrecognised. Only later, when scientists such as Louis Pasteur showed that germs cause disease, was his work understood. Today he is remembered as a pioneer of hand hygiene.

passages.title: The Boy from Rameswaram
passages.text: A. P. J. Abdul Kalam was born in 1931 in Rameswaram, a small island town in Tamil Nadu. His family was not rich, and as a schoolboy he helped them by distributing newspapers in the early mornings. He watched birds flying over the sea and wondered how they stayed in the air. A teacher who explained flight by drawing a bird on the blackboard and then taking the class to the seashore made a deep impression on him. Kalam studied physics and then aeronautical engineering. He worked for many years in India's space and defence research programmes and played a leading role in developing launch vehicles and missiles. This work earned him the popular title 'Missile Man of India'. In 2002 he was elected President of India, and he served until 2007. Yet what people remember most about Kalam is not his high office but his warmth. He loved meeting students and often told them to dream big, explaining that dreams turn into thoughts and thoughts into action. Even after leaving the Rashtrapati Bhavan, he continued to travel and teach. He died in 2015 while delivering a lecture to students in Shillong, doing what he loved best until the very end.

passages.title: Certificates at the Click of a Button
passages.text: Not long ago, getting a simple government certificate could take several days. A citizen had to visit an office, stand in a queue, fill in a paper form, attach copies of documents and then return again and again to ask whether the certificate was ready. For a farmer or a daily-wage worker, every such visit meant a lost day's income. E-governance has begun to change this picture. Through common service centres and online portals, people can now apply for many certificates, such as community, income and nativity certificates, without visiting the issuing office. The application is scanned and sent electronically to the officer concerned. The applicant receives a message on the mobile phone at each stage, and the approved certificate carries a digital signature, so it can be printed anywhere and checked online. The benefits are clear: less travel, less paperwork and fewer chances for middlemen to demand bribes. However, the system works well only when people know how to use it. Elderly citizens and those with little schooling may still need help, and poor internet connections in some villages can cause delays. Training, awareness campaigns and reliable connectivity are therefore as important as the software itself.

passages.title: Small Wings, Big Work
passages.text: When we think of honeybees, we usually think of honey. But the greatest gift bees give us is not honey at all; it is pollination. Many flowering plants cannot produce fruit or seed unless pollen is carried from one flower to another. As a bee moves from flower to flower collecting nectar, fine grains of pollen stick to the hairs on its body and are carried along. Without realising it, the bee helps the plant to reproduce. Crops such as sunflower, mustard, many vegetables and fruit trees depend heavily on insects for pollination. Farmers who keep bee boxes near their fields often notice better yields. In this sense, a single hive can be worth far more to a village than the honey it produces. Unfortunately, bee populations in many parts of the world are under pressure. The careless use of pesticides, the loss of wild flowers and changes in climate all make it harder for bees to survive. Scientists warn that if pollinators decline sharply, food supplies could suffer. The solution need not be complicated. Growing native flowering plants, spraying chemicals only when necessary and protecting patches of wild land can all help these small workers to continue their big work.

passages.title: Silambam: The Dance of the Staff
passages.text: Silambam is one of the oldest martial arts of Tamil Nadu. Its main weapon is a long staff, traditionally cut from bamboo, which the player whirls around the body at great speed. References to the staff and to trained fighters appear in old Tamil literature, and for centuries Silambam was practised by village youth both for self-defence and for display at temple festivals. To an onlooker, a good Silambam performance looks almost like a dance. The player's feet move in fixed patterns while the staff spins, strikes and blocks in a blur of motion. Learning it requires patience. Beginners spend many weeks on footwork alone before they are allowed to spin the staff freely. Teachers insist that control matters more than speed, because a careless swing can injure the player as easily as an opponent. During the colonial period the art declined, and for a time it survived mainly in villages. In recent decades, however, it has seen a revival. Schools and sports clubs now offer training, and competitions are held at district and state levels. Supporters say that Silambam builds strength, balance and concentration, and that it connects young people with a living part of their heritage.

passages.title: Why Teenagers Need Sleep
passages.text: Many students believe that sleeping less gives them more time to study. Research on the brain suggests the opposite. During sleep, the brain does not simply switch off. It sorts the information collected during the day, strengthens important memories and clears away waste products. A student who studies late into the night but sleeps only four or five hours may remember less the next day than a classmate who studied for a shorter time and slept well. Health experts commonly recommend that teenagers sleep about eight to ten hours a night. Yet surveys in many countries show that a large number of them sleep far less. Mobile phones are a major reason. The bright screen and the endless flow of messages keep the mind alert, and the habit of checking the phone 'one last time' can easily stretch into an hour. Lack of sleep affects more than marks. Tired teenagers are more likely to feel irritable, to catch infections and to have accidents while cycling or riding. Simple habits can help: going to bed at the same time each night, keeping phones out of the bedroom, and avoiding heavy meals late in the evening. Sleep, in short, is not wasted time; it is part of learning.

passages.title: The Grand Anicut
passages.text: On the river Kaveri, not far from Tiruchirappalli, stands a structure that has been doing its job for nearly two thousand years. It is the Kallanai, also known as the Grand Anicut, believed to have been built by the Chola king Karikalan. Its purpose was simple but vital: to divert the waters of the Kaveri into the fertile delta so that farmers could irrigate their fields. What is striking about the Kallanai is the method used to build it. The builders placed huge unshaped stones across the sandy riverbed. As the river flowed, the stones settled deeper into the sand and held one another firmly in place. Clay was used to seal the gaps. No cement and no steel were used, yet the structure has outlasted empires. In the nineteenth century, the British engineer Arthur Cotton studied the Kallanai closely and admired its design. Lessons learnt from it influenced later irrigation works in South India. The old structure has since been strengthened and raised, but its ancient core remains. The Kallanai reminds us that great engineering is not only about modern machines. It is about understanding nature closely: the behaviour of water, sand and stone. The early Tamil builders had that understanding, and the farmers of the delta still benefit from it.

passages.title: Back to the Cloth Bag
passages.text: A plastic carry bag may be used for only a few minutes, but it can remain in the environment for hundreds of years. It does not rot like a banana leaf or a paper cover. Instead, it slowly breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics, which have been found in soil, rivers, sea water and even in the stomachs of fish and birds. Discarded plastic causes many other problems. It blocks drains and canals, so that rainwater floods streets during heavy showers. Cattle that eat vegetable waste along with plastic covers can fall ill. Burning plastic to get rid of it releases harmful smoke into the air we breathe. Recognising these dangers, Tamil Nadu banned a number of single-use plastic items, such as carry bags and plastic cups, from January 2019. Along with the ban, people were encouraged to return to traditional alternatives: cloth bags, steel tumblers, and leaves for packing and serving food. The yellow cloth bag, once a common sight in every household, became a symbol of this effort. Laws alone, however, cannot solve the problem. A ban succeeds only when shopkeepers and customers change their habits. Carrying a cloth bag when we go shopping may seem a small step, but when millions of people take it, the effect is enormous.

passages.title: The Hidden Hunger
passages.text: A child may eat three meals a day and still suffer from a kind of hunger. Doctors sometimes call it 'hidden hunger': a lack of important vitamins and minerals in a diet that seems to give enough food. One of the most common forms of hidden hunger is anaemia caused by a shortage of iron. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the substance in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body. When there is too little iron, the body cannot carry enough oxygen. The person feels tired and weak, finds it hard to concentrate, and may look pale. In children, anaemia can affect growth and performance at school. In pregnant women, it can endanger both mother and baby. The good news is that anaemia can often be prevented with simple changes. Green leafy vegetables such as drumstick leaves and other greens, along with pulses, jaggery and dates, are good sources of iron. Eating fruits rich in vitamin C, such as amla, guava or lemon, helps the body absorb iron better. Drinking tea or coffee immediately after meals, on the other hand, can reduce absorption. Regular deworming and, where advised by doctors, iron tablets also play an important role.

passages.title: Marie Curie
passages.text: Maria Sklodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867. At that time women in her country were not allowed to study at the university, so she joined a secret 'floating university' where classes moved from house to house. Later she went to Paris, where she studied physics and mathematics while living in a cold attic room and often going without proper meals. In Paris she met and married Pierre Curie, a scientist who shared her passion for research. Together they studied a strange property of some minerals: they gave off invisible rays. Marie called this property 'radioactivity'. After years of hard work in a poorly equipped shed, the Curies discovered two new elements. Marie named the first one polonium, after her homeland, Poland, and the second radium. In 1903 Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry. She remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. During the First World War, she helped equip vehicles with X-ray machines so that wounded soldiers could be examined near the battlefield. Her long exposure to radiation, whose dangers were not then understood, damaged her health, and she died in 1934.

passages.title: The Right to Know
passages.text: In a democracy, the government works with public money and on behalf of the people. It is therefore reasonable that people should be able to know how decisions are made and how money is spent. The Right to Information Act, 2005, gives every citizen of India the legal right to ask for information held by public authorities. Using the Act is fairly simple. A citizen writes an application to the Public Information Officer of the office concerned, pays a small fee and describes the information required. No reason has to be given for asking. In general, the officer must reply within thirty days. If the information concerns the life or liberty of a person, it must be provided within forty-eight hours. If the citizen is not satisfied with the reply, an appeal can be made. Some information is exempt from disclosure, for example matters affecting the security of the country. Within these limits, however, the Act has been used by ordinary people to find out about delayed pensions, ration supplies, road works and examination results. When officials know that their decisions may be questioned, they tend to act more carefully. In this way, the Act has become an important tool for transparency and accountability in public life.

passages.title: Two Monsoons
passages.text: For most of India, the word 'monsoon' brings to mind the rains of June to September. During these months, moist winds blowing from the south-west over the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal bring heavy rain to large parts of the country. Farmers depend on this south-west monsoon to sow crops such as rice, cotton and pulses. Tamil Nadu, however, has a different pattern. Much of the state lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats during the south-west monsoon, so it receives comparatively little rain in those months. Its main rainy season comes later, from October to December, with the north-east monsoon. As the winds reverse and blow from the north-east across the Bay of Bengal, they pick up moisture and bring rain to the coastal districts. Cyclones that form in the Bay during this season can add heavy downpours. This difference matters a great deal. Reservoirs and tanks in Tamil Nadu are filled largely by the north-east monsoon, and the crop calendar of many districts is planned around it. When the north-east monsoon fails, drinking water shortages can follow in the summer. When it is unusually strong, cities such as Chennai may face flooding. Understanding both monsoons is therefore essential for planning water use in the state.

passages.title: Digging at Keezhadi
passages.text: Keezhadi is a small village in Sivaganga district, a short distance from Madurai on the banks of the Vaigai. For a long time it was known only for its coconut groves. Then, in 2015, archaeologists began careful excavations there, and the soil started to reveal the remains of an ancient settlement. The diggers found brick walls, drains, wells built of terracotta rings, and floors of what may have been workshops. They also found beads, spindle whorls used for spinning thread, dice, and a large number of pottery pieces. Many of the potsherds carry letters in Tamil-Brahmi, an early script used to write Tamil. Some of them seem to bear personal names, suggesting that writing was not limited to kings or priests but was known to ordinary people too. These discoveries are important because they show an organised urban life in the Vaigai valley during the Sangam age. Sangam poems describe busy towns, markets and crafts; Keezhadi gives physical evidence that such places existed. A museum has been opened near the site so that visitors can see the finds for themselves. Archaeology is slow and patient work. Every layer of soil must be recorded before the next is removed. Yet, as Keezhadi shows, such patience can rewrite our understanding of the past.

passages.title: The Colour of the Sea
passages.text: In 1921, a young Indian physicist was returning from Europe by ship. As he stood on the deck and gazed at the deep blue Mediterranean Sea, a question came to his mind: why is the sea blue? The common answer of the time was that the sea simply reflects the blue of the sky. C. V. Raman was not satisfied. Using a small instrument he had carried with him, he made observations on the voyage itself and began to suspect that the water was scattering light in its own way. Back in Calcutta, Raman and his colleagues studied how light is scattered when it passes through liquids and other transparent substances. On 28 February 1928, they reported a new discovery: when light passes through a substance, a tiny part of the scattered light changes its colour, that is, its wavelength. This came to be called the Raman Effect. It gave scientists a new way of studying the structure of molecules. In 1930 Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics. He was the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize in a science subject. Remarkably, his work was done in India with fairly simple equipment. In honour of his discovery, 28 February is celebrated every year in India as National Science Day. Raman's story shows that curiosity about everyday things can lead to great discoveries.

passages.title: A Book for All People
passages.text: Few books have been read, quoted and loved for as long as the Thirukkural. Written by Thiruvalluvar, it contains 1,330 short couplets arranged in 133 chapters of ten couplets each. The work is divided into three sections: Aram, on virtue; Porul, on wealth and public life; and Inbam, on love. Each couplet is only two lines long, yet it often holds a complete idea. This brevity makes the Kural easy to remember and to quote. Teachers use it to explain good conduct, lawyers quote it on justice, and politicians cite it on the duties of a ruler. Its advice on gratitude, patience, truthfulness and hard work is as useful today as it was centuries ago. What has helped the Thirukkural travel across the world is its universal outlook. It does not speak in the name of any one caste, region or religion. Its lessons are addressed to every human being. For this reason it is often called 'Ulaga Podhu Marai', the common scripture of the world. It has been translated into many languages, and new translations continue to appear. At Kanyakumari, at the southern tip of India, a tall statue of Thiruvalluvar stands on a small rock in the sea. Its height of 133 feet was chosen to match the 133 chapters of his work, a fitting tribute to a poet whose words still guide millions.

passages.title: Catching the Rain
passages.text: Every year, a great deal of rain falls on the roofs and roads of our towns and simply runs away into drains. A few months later, the same towns face water shortages, and borewells have to be dug deeper and deeper. Rainwater harvesting is a simple way of breaking this cycle. The idea is to collect rainwater where it falls and either store it or send it into the ground. Water from a rooftop can be led through pipes into a sump for later use. Alternatively, it can be directed into a recharge pit filled with layers of pebbles, gravel and sand. The layers filter the water as it seeps down to join the groundwater below. Over time, this raises the water table and improves the yield of nearby wells. Tamil Nadu was among the first states in India to make rainwater harvesting structures compulsory for buildings, in 2003. In many neighbourhoods, residents noticed that water levels in their wells rose and that the water became less salty. The success depended, however, on proper maintenance. A pit filled with silt or a pipe blocked with leaves cannot do its job. Rainwater harvesting is not new. The tanks and ponds built by our ancestors in villages served the same purpose. Reviving that wisdom, with the help of modern methods, can secure water for the future.

passages.title: Two Drops of Protection
passages.text: Polio is a disease caused by a virus that mainly affects young children. In some cases it attacks the nerves and causes paralysis, often of the legs, which may last for life. There is no cure once paralysis sets in, but the disease can be prevented by vaccination. For many years India had one of the highest numbers of polio cases in the world. To change this, the country launched the Pulse Polio campaign in the mid-1990s. On fixed days, children below five years of age were given oral polio drops at booths set up in schools, health centres, bus stands and railway stations. Health workers then went from house to house to find children who had been missed. Millions of volunteers, including teachers and students, joined the effort. The work was difficult. Some families were afraid of the vaccine because of rumours, and some areas were hard to reach because of floods or poor roads. Patient explanation by local leaders and health workers gradually built trust. India's last case of wild polio was reported in January 2011. In 2014, the country was officially certified polio-free. The success showed that, with steady effort and public cooperation, even a large and diverse country can defeat a disease. Vaccination drops are still given, however, so that the virus does not return.

passages.title: The Long Walk to Freedom
passages.text: Nelson Mandela was born in 1918 in a small village in South Africa. At that time the country was ruled by a white minority, and black South Africans were denied the right to vote and many other basic rights. Later a harsh system called apartheid separated people by race in housing, education and even public places. Mandela trained as a lawyer and joined the struggle against this injustice. Because of his activities he was arrested, and in 1964 he was sentenced to life imprisonment. He spent the next twenty-seven years in prison, much of it on Robben Island, where prisoners broke stones in harsh conditions. Yet Mandela did not allow bitterness to control him. He studied, encouraged fellow prisoners and even learnt the language of those who had imprisoned him, so that he could understand them better. He was released in 1990. Instead of seeking revenge, he worked with the government to end apartheid peacefully. In 1993 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize, and in 1994, in the country's first election in which all races could vote, he became South Africa's first black President. Mandela believed that hatred is learnt, and that if people can learn to hate, they can also be taught to love. His life shows how forgiveness can be a source of strength rather than weakness.

passages.title: The Village Parliament
passages.text: Democracy is often thought of as something that happens in Parliament or the State Assembly. But one of its most direct forms can be seen in villages, in the Gram Sabha. The Gram Sabha is not a small committee; it is made up of all the adults in the village whose names are on the electoral roll. Every voter is a member. Meetings of the Gram Sabha are held on fixed days each year, such as Republic Day and Independence Day, and on other occasions when needed. At these meetings, the village panchayat presents its accounts and explains the work it has done. Villagers can ask questions about roads, drinking water, street lights and schemes for the poor. They can suggest which works should be taken up first and help choose the people who should benefit from welfare schemes. The strength of the Gram Sabha lies in participation. When only a few people attend, the meeting becomes a formality and decisions may be taken by a small group. When many villagers, including women and the poor, attend and speak, the panchayat is more likely to be honest and responsive. In this sense the Gram Sabha is a kind of village parliament, where the people themselves keep watch over those they have elected.

passages.title: Power from the Sun
passages.text: Every day the sun pours enormous amounts of energy onto the earth. For most of human history, we used this energy only indirectly, for drying grain or clothes and for growing crops. Today, solar panels allow us to turn sunlight directly into electricity. A solar panel is made of many small units called solar cells, usually built from silicon. When sunlight falls on a cell, it causes tiny particles called electrons to move, and this flow of electrons is an electric current. The panels have no moving parts, make no noise and give out no smoke while working. India, with its long hours of sunshine, is well suited to solar power. Large solar parks spread over hundreds of acres now feed electricity into the grid. At the same time, small rooftop systems are being installed on homes, schools and offices. A farmer can run a solar water pump in the field without waiting for grid power. Solar energy has its limitations. Panels produce no electricity at night and less on cloudy days, so the energy must either be stored in batteries or supplemented from other sources. Old panels must also be disposed of carefully. Even so, as the cost of panels has fallen, solar power has become one of the most promising ways of meeting our energy needs while reducing pollution.

passages.title: Stories in Stone at Mamallapuram
passages.text: About fifty kilometres south of Chennai, on the shore of the Bay of Bengal, lies Mamallapuram, also called Mahabalipuram. In the seventh and eighth centuries, it was an important port of the Pallava kings. The town takes its name from Narasimhavarman I, a Pallava ruler who bore the title 'Mamalla', meaning 'great wrestler'. The Pallava sculptors turned the rocky landscape of the town into an open-air gallery. They cut cave temples into hillsides and carved five free-standing shrines, known as the Pancha Rathas, each from a single mass of rock. On a huge rock face they created a crowded scene of gods, people, animals and a river flowing down a natural cleft. This relief is popularly known as Arjuna's Penance, though some scholars interpret it as the descent of the Ganga. Near the sea stands the Shore Temple, built of cut stone, which has faced wind and salt spray for more than a thousand years. In 1984 the group of monuments at Mamallapuram was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The town is also known today for its living tradition of stone carving. Young sculptors still learn the craft there, and the sound of chisel on stone continues the story the Pallavas began.

passages.title: The Poet of Freedom
passages.text: Subramania Bharati, lovingly called Bharathiyar, was born in 1882 at Ettayapuram in present-day Thoothukudi district. Even as a boy he showed such a gift for poetry that he was given the title 'Bharati'. He went on to become one of the greatest Tamil poets of modern times. Bharathiyar lived during the freedom struggle, and his songs filled people with courage. He wrote of a free India at a time when such hopes seemed distant. He also worked as a journalist and used his writing to criticise injustice. Because of his views he faced hardship and, for some years, lived in Puducherry, which was then under French rule, to escape arrest by the British. His concerns went beyond political freedom. He spoke out strongly against caste discrimination and demanded education and equal rights for women. His idea of the 'new woman' was of one who walks with her head held high and fears no one. He also wrote simple, joyful songs for children and loving poems about nature. Bharathiyar died in 1921, at the age of only thirty-nine, without seeing the freedom he had dreamt of. Yet his words live on. His songs are sung in schools, at public functions and in films, and his vision of a just and equal society continues to inspire.

passages.title: The Mansions of Chettinad
passages.text: In the dry country around Karaikudi in southern Tamil Nadu, travellers are often surprised to find villages full of enormous mansions. These are the houses of Chettinad, built mostly in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries by the Nattukottai Chettiar community, who had grown wealthy through trade and banking in Burma, Ceylon and South-East Asia. The merchants spent their fortunes on homes that combined local skill with materials brought from far away. Long corridors open onto large central courtyards that let in light and air while keeping the rooms cool. Pillars of polished wood, Italian marble and coloured glass from Europe can be seen in many houses. The floors are often covered with Athangudi tiles, handmade locally using sand, cement and natural colours, and dried slowly without being fired in a kiln. Many of these mansions now stand empty, as families have moved to cities. Some have fallen into decay, and their wooden pillars and doors have been sold off. Others have been restored as heritage hotels, attracting visitors who come to see the architecture and taste the region's famous spicy cuisine. Conservationists argue that the houses are not just private property but a shared heritage that tells the story of a trading community's journeys across the seas.

passages.title: Gardens Under the Sea
passages.text: Coral reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. Although they cover only a tiny part of the ocean floor, they provide shelter and food to a huge variety of fish, crabs, sea turtles and other creatures. In India, important reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, between the southern coast of Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, as well as around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep. A coral reef may look like rock, but it is built by living animals. Tiny creatures called coral polyps produce hard skeletons of limestone, and over thousands of years these skeletons pile up into reefs. Inside the polyps live microscopic algae that make food using sunlight and also give corals their bright colours. The coral and the algae depend on each other. When the sea becomes too warm, this partnership breaks down. The corals push out the algae, lose their colour and turn white. This is called coral bleaching. If the water cools soon, the corals may recover; if not, they can die. Pollution, destructive fishing and the removal of coral for building also harm reefs. Healthy reefs protect coastlines by breaking the force of waves, and they support the fishing families who live along the shore. Protecting them is therefore important for both nature and people.

passages.title: A Silent Epidemic
passages.text: Diabetes was once thought of as a disease of the rich and the elderly. Today it affects people of all income groups, and doctors are seeing it in younger and younger patients. Because it may develop for years without obvious symptoms, it is sometimes called a silent disease. In diabetes, the level of sugar in the blood stays higher than normal. Normally, a hormone called insulin, made by the pancreas, helps the body's cells take in sugar from the blood and use it for energy. In the most common form of diabetes, the body does not respond properly to insulin, or does not make enough of it. Over time, high blood sugar can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart. Some risk factors, such as family history and age, cannot be changed. Others can. Lack of physical activity, excess body weight and a diet heavy in sweets, refined flour and sugary drinks all increase the risk. A brisk walk of about half an hour on most days, meals with more vegetables, pulses and whole grains, and limits on sugar can make a real difference. Since the disease may be silent at first, regular check-ups are important, especially for people with a family history. Early detection allows treatment to begin before serious damage is done.

passages.title: The Lady with the Lamp
passages.text: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820 into a wealthy British family. In those days, nursing was not considered a respectable job for a woman of her class. Hospitals were often dirty, and nurses received little training. Florence, however, felt a strong call to care for the sick, and against her family's wishes she trained as a nurse. In 1854, during the Crimean War, she was sent with a team of nurses to a military hospital at Scutari. What she found there shocked her. Wounded soldiers lay in crowded, filthy wards with poor food and little clean water. More men were dying of infections than of their battle wounds. Florence and her nurses cleaned the wards, organised proper food and laundry, and demanded better supplies. Over the following months the death rate fell considerably. At night she walked through the long wards carrying a lamp to check on the patients, and the soldiers began to call her 'the Lady with the Lamp'. After the war, she used careful records and charts to convince the government that hospitals needed reform. In 1860 she established a training school for nurses in London. Nightingale turned nursing into a respected profession. Today, International Nurses Day is observed on 12 May, her birthday, in honour of her contribution.

passages.title: Don't Share That OTP
passages.text: As more of our banking, shopping and government services move online, a new kind of crime has grown alongside: cyber fraud. The criminals rarely need to break into computers. More often, they simply trick people into giving away information. A common trick goes like this. A person receives a call from someone claiming to be a bank officer. The caller says that the person's account will be blocked unless certain details are 'verified' at once. The victim is then asked to share the one-time password, or OTP, that has just arrived on the phone. Once the OTP is shared, money can be taken from the account within minutes. Other tricks include messages announcing a lottery prize, links to fake websites that look like real ones, and requests to install an app that lets a stranger control the phone. The basic rules of safety are simple. Banks and government offices never ask for an OTP, PIN or password over the phone. A message that creates panic or promises an unexpectedly large reward should be treated with suspicion. Links should be opened only from trusted sources. If someone is cheated, they should report it immediately to the bank and to the police cyber crime cell, because quick action can sometimes stop the money from being withdrawn. Technology makes life easier, but only an alert user can make it safe.

passages.title: The Blue Mountains' Living Treasure
passages.text: In 1986 India set up its first biosphere reserve in the Nilgiris. The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve spreads across parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, covering forests, grasslands and hills of the Western Ghats. It includes well-known protected areas such as Mudumalai, Mukurthi and Silent Valley. A biosphere reserve is different from an ordinary sanctuary. It is planned in zones. The core zone is strictly protected and is left largely undisturbed. Around it lies a buffer zone, where limited activities such as research and education are allowed. The outer transition zone includes villages and farms, where people live and work in ways that try to support conservation. The idea is to protect nature while recognising that human communities are part of the landscape. The Nilgiri reserve is rich in life. Elephants, tigers and gaur roam its forests. On the high grassy slopes lives the Nilgiri tahr, a mountain goat that is the state animal of Tamil Nadu. Many plants and animals here are found nowhere else in the world. Tribal communities such as the Todas, Kotas and Irulas have lived in these hills for generations, and their knowledge of forests and medicinal plants is an important part of the region's heritage.

passages.title: Threads of Gold
passages.text: In the temple town of Kanchipuram, the sound of handlooms has been heard for centuries. The town's silk sarees are famous across India and are worn by many brides on their wedding day. Their fame rests on three qualities: heavy, lustrous silk, rich borders woven with zari, and bold contrasting colours. A Kanchipuram saree is woven from pure mulberry silk. The zari, a thread made by twisting fine silver wire with silk and coating it with gold, is woven into the borders and the decorated end-piece called the pallu. In many traditional sarees, the body and the border are woven separately and then interlocked so firmly that the border will not come apart even if the saree tears. This method, known as korvai, needs great skill and often two or three weavers working together at one loom. A single saree can take many days or even weeks to complete, depending on the design. Because of its special identity, the Kanchipuram silk saree has received a Geographical Indication tag, which means that only sarees made in the region by the traditional method can be sold under that name. Weavers today face competition from cheaper power-loom imitations. Buyers who choose genuine handloom sarees help keep this ancient craft, and the families who practise it, alive.

passages.title: The Man Who Knew Infinity
passages.text: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born in 1887 in Erode and grew up in Kumbakonam in Tamil Nadu. As a schoolboy he was fascinated by numbers. When he came across a book that listed thousands of mathematical results without full explanations, he worked through them on his own and then went far beyond them. His single-minded love of mathematics came at a cost. He neglected other subjects, failed college examinations and lost his scholarship. For some years he lived in poverty, filling notebooks with formulas while searching for work. Eventually he found a job as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust, where some officials recognised his talent and encouraged him. In 1913 he wrote to the English mathematician G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, enclosing pages of his results. Hardy realised that the writer was a genius and invited him to England. There the two worked together and published important papers. In 1918 Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the highest honours for a scientist. The cold climate and unfamiliar food in England affected his health. He returned to India and died in 1920, at the age of just thirty-two. Mathematicians are still studying the ideas in his notebooks. His birthday, 22 December, is celebrated in India as National Mathematics Day.

passages.title: A Festival of Thanks
passages.text: In the middle of January, as the Tamil month of Thai begins, villages and towns across Tamil Nadu celebrate Pongal. It is a harvest festival, a time to thank the sun, the rain, the cattle and all those who help the farmer bring in the crop. The celebrations usually last four days. On Bhogi, the first day, old and unwanted things are discarded and houses are cleaned and decorated, as a sign of making a fresh start. The second day, Thai Pongal, is the main day. Families boil newly harvested rice with milk and jaggery in a new pot, often in the open courtyard facing the sun. When the milk boils over, people joyfully shout 'Pongalo Pongal!', for the overflowing pot is a symbol of plenty. The third day, Mattu Pongal, is dedicated to cattle, which help in ploughing and give milk. Cows and bullocks are bathed, their horns are painted and they are decorated with bells and garlands. On the fourth day, Kaanum Pongal, families visit relatives and friends and go on outings together. In recent years, people have been encouraged to celebrate Bhogi without burning tyres and plastics, which pollute the air. The spirit of the festival, after all, is gratitude to nature, and caring for the environment is the truest way of expressing it.

passages.title: The Village That Protects Birds
passages.text: Every winter, thousands of birds arrive at a small lake near the village of Vedanthangal in Chengalpattu district. Herons, egrets, storks, cormorants and many other water birds nest in the trees that stand in the water. Some come from nearby wetlands; others travel long distances to breed here. Vedanthangal is among the oldest bird sanctuaries in India. The sanctuary owes its existence largely to the villagers. For generations, local farmers have protected the nesting birds. Their reason was practical as well as kind. The droppings of the birds fall into the lake and enrich the water with nutrients. When this water is used to irrigate the surrounding paddy fields, it acts as a natural fertiliser and improves the harvest. Protecting the birds therefore meant protecting the farmers' own fields. This partnership between people and wildlife is a valuable lesson. Conservation is often imagined as something that keeps people away from nature. At Vedanthangal, people and birds have shared the same space for a long time, each benefiting the other. Today the sanctuary also attracts visitors and students. To keep it healthy, the lake must receive enough water during the monsoon, and the trees in which the birds nest must be cared for. Loud noise and plastic litter can disturb the birds, so visitors are expected to behave responsibly.

passages.title: When Medicines Stop Working
passages.text: The discovery of antibiotics in the twentieth century was one of the greatest advances in medicine. Infections that had once killed people, such as those from wounds or pneumonia, could suddenly be cured. Today, however, doctors warn that this precious weapon is losing its power. Antibiotics work against bacteria. Each time they are used, most of the bacteria are killed, but a few that happen to be resistant may survive and multiply. Over time, these resistant bacteria can spread, and infections caused by them become hard or even impossible to treat. This is called antibiotic resistance. The careless use of antibiotics speeds up the process. Many people take them for colds and flu, which are caused by viruses, not bacteria; in such cases the medicine does no good but still encourages resistance. Others stop a course of antibiotics as soon as they feel better, leaving the toughest bacteria alive. Buying antibiotics without a prescription and using them freely in poultry and cattle farming add to the problem. Each of us can help. Antibiotics should be taken only when a qualified doctor prescribes them, and the full course should be completed as advised. Washing hands, keeping vaccinations up to date and maintaining clean surroundings reduce infections and therefore reduce the need for antibiotics.

passages.title: A Doctor Who Fought for Women
passages.text: Muthulakshmi Reddy was born in 1886 in Pudukkottai. At a time when few girls went to school, her father supported her education. She went on to study medicine at the Madras Medical College and became one of the first women doctors in the Madras Presidency. Her work as a doctor showed her how much women and children suffered from poverty, ill-health and unjust social customs. She believed that medicine alone could not solve these problems; laws and attitudes had to change too. In 1927 she was nominated to the Madras Legislative Council, becoming one of the first women legislators in India. There she worked for reforms such as raising the age of marriage for girls and ending the devadasi system, under which young girls were dedicated to temples and often exploited. Muthulakshmi Reddy also founded institutions that are still active. She started the Avvai Home in Chennai to give shelter and education to girls and women who had no one to support them. Later, moved by the death of her sister from cancer, she worked to establish the Cancer Institute at Adyar, which grew into a major centre for treatment and research. Her life shows that a professional skill can become a tool for social change when it is joined with courage and compassion.

passages.title: The Golden Hour
passages.text: Every year, road accidents in India kill and injure a very large number of people, many of them young. Behind each number is a family that has lost a breadwinner, a student or a child. Most of these accidents are not caused by bad luck but by human behaviour that can be changed. Speeding is one of the biggest causes. At higher speed, a driver has less time to react and the force of a collision is much greater. Driving after drinking alcohol, using a mobile phone while driving, jumping signals and driving on the wrong side are other common causes. For two-wheeler riders, a properly fastened helmet greatly reduces the risk of head injury, and for those in cars, seat belts can save lives. When an accident does happen, the first hour after the injury is often called the 'golden hour'. Prompt medical care during this period can make the difference between life and death. Unfortunately, bystanders sometimes hesitate to help because they fear being troubled by the police or courts. To encourage help, the law now protects 'Good Samaritans' who, in good faith, take accident victims to hospital. They cannot be forced to reveal their identity or to pay hospital charges. Road safety is not only the duty of the traffic police. Every road user, whether driver, rider or pedestrian, shares the responsibility.

passages.title: The Farmer's Friend
passages.text: Charles Darwin, famous for his theory of evolution, spent many years studying a much humbler creature: the earthworm. He concluded that few animals have played so important a part in the history of the world. Farmers in many lands have long agreed, calling the earthworm 'the farmer's friend'. Earthworms live in moist soil and feed on dead leaves and other decaying matter. As they burrow, they swallow soil along with this matter and pass it out as fine, crumbly casts that are rich in nutrients. In this way they turn waste into natural fertiliser. Their tunnels also loosen the soil, allowing air and water to reach the roots of plants and helping rainwater soak in rather than run off. The excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, however, can harm earthworms and reduce their numbers. Soil that has lost its earthworms tends to become hard and less fertile. Many farmers and gardeners now practise vermicomposting. Kitchen and farm waste, such as vegetable peels and dry leaves, is placed in pits or tanks with earthworms, which convert it into rich compost within a few weeks. This method reduces waste, saves money on fertilisers and improves the soil. It shows how a small creature, often ignored, can help solve big problems.

passages.title: Water at the Pump
passages.text: Helen Keller was born in 1880 in Alabama, in the United States. When she was about nineteen months old, a severe illness left her unable to see or hear. Cut off from the world, she grew into a wild and frustrated child who could not understand others or make herself understood. When Helen was nearly seven, her parents engaged a young teacher, Anne Sullivan, who had herself suffered from poor eyesight. Anne began spelling words into Helen's palm with her fingers. At first Helen copied the movements without understanding that they meant anything. The breakthrough came one day at a water pump. As cool water flowed over one of Helen's hands, Anne spelled 'w-a-t-e-r' into the other. Suddenly Helen understood that the movements stood for the thing she was feeling. That day she learnt many new words, and her eager journey of learning began. Helen went on to learn to read Braille and even to speak. In 1904 she graduated from Radcliffe College, the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree. She became a writer and a speaker, travelling to many countries, including India, to work for the rights and welfare of people with disabilities. Helen Keller's life reminds us that with patient teaching and a determined spirit, barriers that seem impossible can be overcome.

passages.title: The Doctor on the Screen
passages.text: For many people in remote villages, seeing a specialist doctor has meant a long and expensive journey to a city hospital. Travel costs, lost wages and the difficulty of leaving the family often force patients to delay treatment until the illness becomes serious. Telemedicine offers a way to bring the doctor closer. In telemedicine, a patient consults a doctor through a video or audio call, using a mobile phone, a computer or a terminal at a nearby health centre. A health worker at the centre may help by measuring blood pressure or sugar levels and sharing the readings. The doctor can then advise treatment and send an electronic prescription. India's government runs a national telemedicine service of this kind, and its use grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, when people were advised to avoid crowded hospitals. Telemedicine has clear advantages: it saves time and money, reduces crowding in hospitals and allows follow-up visits without travel. It also has limits. A doctor cannot carry out a full physical examination over a screen, and some conditions need tests or emergency care that only a hospital can provide. Poor internet connections can interrupt consultations, and some patients find the technology hard to use. Telemedicine is therefore best seen not as a replacement for hospitals but as a useful bridge between the patient and the doctor.

one of the first people to develop a new idea
